opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it comes from where I sit. At NVIDIA, our job is fundamentally to enable other people. We build the platform, the chips, the software stack, and now with things like world foundation models, the base models that other people build on top of. So if someone is training a robot, or building an autonomous driving system, or doing video generation, my first instinct isn't "they're competing with us." It's "how can we help them succeed?" Because if they succeed, the whole field moves forward, and that's good for everyone, including us.

The other part is more personal. I came from academia, and in research, the culture is very open. You publish your work, other people build on it, they cite you, you build on theirs. Progress really is cumulative. I've seen how much faster things move when people share. Generative AI is a great example: so many of the ideas came from different groups, different companies, and they all kind of stacked together. If everyone had been secretive and defensive, we'd be much further behind.

Also, honestly, the problems we're working on, like physical AI and getting machines to understand and act in the real world, are just enormous. No single company or lab is going to solve them alone. The space is so big that thinking in terms of competition feels a bit small. It's more useful to ask: what's the piece that we're uniquely positioned to contribute? For us, that's often the infrastructure and the foundation models. Then we open them up, let developers fine-tune them, and see what people create.

And practically speaking, it makes life simpler. If you see everyone as a competitor, you spend a lot of energy worrying and guarding. If you see people as partners or customers, you spend that energy listening to what they need. That tends to make you build better things. So for me, it's both a philosophy and, I think, just a better way to do the work.

r001.rationale: He says NVIDIA builds platforms and models to enable others, and that their success moves the field forward and benefits everyone, including NVIDIA.

r002.rationale: He describes building tools that help others succeed and says shared work makes progress move faster.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes from the position NVIDIA is in, and honestly from how I see the field. We build platforms. The whole point of a platform is that other people build on top of it, so if someone is doing great work in generative AI or world models, I don't look at that and think, "they're taking something from us." I think, "how do we help them run faster on our hardware, how do we learn from what they're doing, and where can we work together?" Almost everyone doing serious AI research today is either a customer, a collaborator, or a potential one, and treating them otherwise would just be bad for us and bad for the field.

There's also a more personal side. I came up through research, and research only works because people share. The breakthroughs I care about, in simulation, in physical AI, in teaching models how the world actually works, are much bigger than any single lab. If I spent my energy worrying about who is ahead this quarter, I'd miss the fact that the real problem is still mostly unsolved. Robots still can't reliably do what a child can do. That's humbling, and it makes competition feel like the wrong frame.

So my attitude is pretty simple. Be genuinely useful to people, be open about what we've learned, and assume that if the whole ecosystem gets stronger, we'll be fine. I'd rather be the person everyone wants to work with than the person everyone is trying to beat.

r001.rationale: He explains that NVIDIA builds a platform others can build on and help them run faster, and says a stronger ecosystem benefits NVIDIA too. This conveys confidence that what he builds can help others.

r002.rationale: He explicitly says the platform’s purpose is to help others run faster on NVIDIA hardware, communicating the objective of enabling others to advance faster.

astra-6.text:
For me, it starts with asking, “What can we build together?” People working on similar problems may have different strengths, and something we develop could help them, just as their work could help us. So I try to understand what they need and where we can contribute.

That doesn’t mean competition disappears. But if I see everyone primarily as a competitor, I’m focused on protecting what I have. If I see them as a potential customer or partner, I’m focused on creating something useful. I think that’s a more productive mindset, especially in a field where there’s still so much to figure out.

r001.rationale: The response says something developed together could help people working on similar problems, but it does not attribute the attitude to confidence that his work can help everyone.

r002.rationale: The response describes creating something useful, but it does not identify helping everyone advance faster as an objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it starts with curiosity. When I meet someone working on a similar problem, my first question is: what can we learn from each other? They may understand a customer need that we have missed, or have a capability that complements ours. There may be an opportunity to work together.

Of course, competition exists. But if you look at every interaction through that lens, you can become defensive and miss opportunities. I prefer to focus on creating value: can we help this person, can they help us, or can we build something useful together? That is what I mean by treating people as potential customers or partners. It keeps the relationship open, even when we happen to compete in one area.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes curiosity, mutual learning, and creating value, but does not attribute this attitude to confidence that what Ming-Yu Liu builds can help everyone.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions building something useful together, but does not identify helping everyone advance faster as an objective.
